title: Weighty matters

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The field of human weight loss is infinitely complex. The findings by public health experts, physicians, psychologists, molecular biologists and nutritionists are frequently at odds. 'Everyone subscribes to their own little theory,' says Robert Berkowitz, medical director at the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine. Nonetheless, a few patterns are beginning to stand out more clearly.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Many of us could attest to the fact that the human body resists weight change. We're each born with a predetermined weight range and the further we push our bodies away from it, the more intensely the body fights back. Some people on a diet find that their bodies go into a state of chronic hunger, a feeling that Rudolph Leibel, a researcher at Columbia University, likens to extreme thirst. 'A few of us might be able to tolerate this, but the majority couldn't stand it,' says Leibel. Rather than a lack of will power in dieters, Leibel blames our genes and cites research suggesting that 6 per cent of obese children and adults can trace their condition to some sort of defect in their innate makeup.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Moderate daily exercise has long been recommended but may in practice make minimal difference. 'Radical alterations are necessary,' says Deirdre Barrett, a psychologist at Harvard. 'People don't lose weight by taking a little walk every day or choosing the small portion of French fries.' Barrett refers to members of the National Weight Control Registry (NWCR), a group of more than 5,000 people who have not only lost weight, but have kept it off so far. They all had one thing in common – vigorous exercise for an hour or longer every day.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That said, not everyone can lose 30 kilograms and not everyone needs to. The goal shouldn't be getting thin, but getting healthy. It may be sufficient to whittle your weight down to the lower end of your predetermined weight range, according to Jeffrey Friedman, a geneticist at Rockefeller University. 'We focus on appearance because that's what everyone notices,' he says, 'but losing even 5 kilograms vastly decreases your risk of diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Your optimal weight may be influenced very early on in life. If a woman has high blood-sugar levels while she's pregnant (known as gestational diabetes), her children are more likely to be overweight or obese, according to a study of 10,000 mother-child pairs. 'The good news,' according to Teresa Hillier of the Kaiser Permanente Centre, 'is that high blood sugar during pregnancy is entirely avoidable – children born to women who sought treatment during pregnancy ended up no fatter than their peers.'

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Of course, we would all love to know exactly which diet works best. A year-long US government-funded study comparing Atkins, LEARN (Lifestyle, Exercise, Attitudes, Relationships and Nutrition, based on the food pyramid), the Zone, and Ornish programmes found all four work more or less. But in every case, the amount of weight loss was modest, and there was no guarantee the weight would not be put back on.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One quite different line of enquiry has been followed by Nikhil Dhurandhar, associate professor at Pennington Biomedical Research Centre, who has asked the question: What if fat is caused not by diet or genes at all, but by common viruses? This idea of 'infectobesity' first came to him 20 years ago when he was a young doctor treating obesity among women in Mumbai. His research, however, did not involve humans but chickens. Dhurandhar discovered that birds infected with a virus called SMAM-1 became obese on the same diet as uninfected birds, which stayed thin. He subsequently found that nearly one in five overweight women in his clinic had been infected with SMAM-1, and that they were about 15 kilograms heavier than those never exposed to it.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: He later moved to the US in order to continue his research, but this time using a different virus to SMAM-1. Dhurandhar found that every species of animal he infected with a strain named AD-36 became obese – chickens, mice, monkeys gained 15 per cent of their body weight upon exposure. His studies showed that the same virus naturally infects around 17 per cent of the human population but is present in 30 per cent of obese people, a figure Dhurandhar believes is highly significant. A company named Obetech offers testing for the virus and, although it cannot be removed from your body, the test can provide you with a warning: if you find out you're infected, you can start eating healthily and exercising now to stave off obesity later. In his latest studies, Dhurandhar has isolated a gene that, when impeded from expressing itself, seems to turn off the virus. He considers this to be a most promising development, and the final goal of this research is to create a sort of vaccine for obesity. It may be a long shot, but for people struggling to lose weight, the possibility of an alternative cause of obesity offers some solace.

groups.title: Professor Dhurandhar's approach
content: Nikhil Dhurandhar was conducting research using {{23}} in Mumbai when he first conceived his theory that obesity could be caused by viruses. After moving to the USA he investigated whether humans infected with the virus named {{24}} had a higher obesity rate than others. At present, detection of the virus can serve as a warning for potential problems. A {{25}} has been identified in his most recent research that seems to block the virus, and Dhurandhar's ultimate aim is the production of a {{26}} of some kind.
